nodes.title: Resolution - read this
widgets_values:
# Resolution

Default is **2048 x 2048**.

## Why a power of two
Game engines build mipmap chains and block compression around powers of
two. 2048 works but produces no clean mip chain and streams badly.
Stick to **1024 / 2048 / 4096**.

For most indie work 2048 is the right call - 4096 quadruples memory for
detail nobody sees at gameplay distance.

## Changing it
Several values must match:

| Field | 2048 | 4096 |
|---|---|---|
| 2. Target Resolution | 2048 | 4096 |
| Offset by half edge (shift_x/y) | 1024 | 2048 |
| Mask base w/h | 2048 | 4096 |
| Vertical bar height | 2048 | 4096 |
| Horizontal bar width | 2048 | 4096 |
| Add vertical bar `x` | 944 | 1968 |
| Add horizontal bar `y` | 944 | 1968 |
| Back to target resolution | 2048 | 4096 |
| Upscale Albedo / Roughness | 2048 | 4096 |
| High-pass Back to target | 2048 | 4096 |
| EmptyImage x3 (Metallic, AO) | 2048 | 4096 |

Formula for the two MaskComposite offsets:
`(resolution - bar width) / 2`

If the offset is wrong the seam does not sit in the centre and tiling
breaks.

Do not exceed the resolution of your source photo. Above that you are
inventing pixels that were never there.

nodes.title: In Blender / Unreal
widgets_values:
# Downstream

## Colour spaces
**Base Color** = sRGB - **everything else** = Non-Color / Raw / Linear

## The normal map is computed, not estimated
It is derived from the height map with a Sobel gradient at full
resolution - no model, no 768 px ceiling. Marigold Normals was removed:
it estimates **scene** normals, and a flat surface shot head-on returns
a flat lavender field, which is correct but useless for texture work.

`normal_intensity` is the strength knob. Default **0.60** - at 2048 px
there is already a lot of detail, so lower values usually read better.
Raise it for shallow surfaces, lower it if the result looks embossed.

`flip_y` turns OpenGL into DirectX if you ever need it here rather than
in `unreal_prep`.

## Unreal
- The normal must be flipped to **DirectX** -> workflow `unreal_prep`
- ORM is already packed here: uncheck `sRGB`, compression `Masks`

## Height as real displacement
Needs subdivision on the object. Keep the strength low (0.01-0.05).

nodes.title: Height, Normal and AO
widgets_values:
# The height chain

Height comes from the **luminance** of the tileable image, then runs
through a **high-pass** filter.

## Why the high-pass
Raw luminance confuses colour with elevation: a white pebble becomes a
hill, a dark one a pit, even though both sit at the same level. The
high-pass strips the large-scale brightness variation and leaves only
local relief.

Bypass the node **High-pass** (Ctrl+B) to compare - image1 passes
straight through, so you get the raw height back.

`blend_factor` on **High-pass contrast** is the strength knob for how
pronounced the relief reads. Default 0.55.

## Normal maps
Both are generated from the high-passed height with a Sobel gradient at
full resolution - no model, no 768 px ceiling.

- `normal_gl` - **OpenGL**, green up. Blender, Cinema 4D, Maya, Godot
- `normal_dx` - **DirectX**, green flipped. Unreal, Unity

`normal_intensity` (default 0.60) is the depth knob. Raise it for
shallow surfaces. `depth_scale` goes up to 2.0 and helps when the height
map has a narrow value range.

## AO
Derived from the cavity of the high-passed height, biased towards white.
It is a **cavity approximation**, not true ambient occlusion - it darkens
crevices, it does not compute light transport.

Most renderers do their own AO. Use this one for mobile, VR, or baked
lighting, and leave it out otherwise. `blend_factor` sets the strength;
0.0 gives a plain white map.

nodes.title: Why a hand-built mask
widgets_values:
# The seam mask

The mask is built from `SolidMask` + `MaskComposite`: a black field with
two white bars forming a cross in the exact centre of the image.

**Why not the `border_mask` output of ImageShift?** With `cyclic = true`
nothing is left blank, so that output returns a full white mask - which
tells the sampler to repaint the entire surface. That is exactly what
goes wrong if you wire it up.

## The one knob that matters
`width` on **Vertical bar** and `height` on **Horizontal bar** set how
wide the repaired band is. 160 px at 2048 is about 8 percent of the
image.

- Too narrow: the seam still shows
- Too wide: you throw away photo detail for no reason

If you change it, the two `MaskComposite` offsets must follow:
`(resolution - bar width) / 2`.

## Denoise
Set to **0.70**, not 1.0. At full denoise the sampler invents freely and
misses the material. Below 0.5 the seam usually survives.

nodes.title: Convert to subgraphs
widgets_values:
# Four groups, four steps

The four coloured groups are cut so that each one becomes exactly one
subgraph.

1. Select the nodes (rubber-band select, not the group title bar)
2. Right click -> **Convert to Subgraph**
3. Select the subgraph -> **Edit Subgraph Widgets**
4. Set the widgets listed below to visible, hide the rest

Convert **back to front**: [D], then [C], [B], [A].

## What belongs on top

**[A] Tile**
- `denoise` and `steps` on the sampler
- `seed`
- `value` / `width` on the two bar masks (seam band width)

**[C] Detail**
- `strength` on Match colour to photo
- `blend_factor` on Detail from photo (sharpness)
- `blend_factor` on Darken (brightness)

**[D] Output**
- the `filename_prefix` fields

Everything else stays inside.

**Why not pre-packed?** The subgraph format changed several times
between frontend versions. Hand-written it loads wrong on some of them.
Converting in the UI always matches your build.

nodes.title: Read first - structure
widgets_values:
# One workflow, four building blocks

```
1. Load photo
2. Target resolution
   |
[A] Tile        offset + seam repair
   |
3. 4. Preview   check here before moving on
   |
[B] Marigold    albedo / roughness / normal at 768
   |
[C] Detail      frequency split, sharpness restored
   |
[D] Output      9 maps + ORM
```

**Why the AI stages run small:** Marigold works at 768, SDXL at 1024.
That is fixed. The output sharpness therefore does **not** come through a
model - it comes straight from the photo. The models only supply the
coarse layer.

The seam is the one exception: there is no original left there, so only
that narrow band gets replaced.

nodes.title: Batch processing
widgets_values:
# Batch processing

The node **BATCH** in the input group is bypassed by default. It turns
the workflow from one-photo-at-a-time into a folder run.

## Switching it on
1. Select the node, press **Ctrl+B** to un-bypass
2. Enter the folder in `directory_path` (absolute path)
3. Drag its `IMAGE` output onto `2. Target Resolution` - this replaces
   the link coming from **1. Load Photo**
4. Set `batch_size` to how many photos per run

## How the index works
`image_index` picks which photo. To walk through a folder, right click
the widget, set it to **increment**, then queue as many runs as you have
photos.

`sort_by` and `sort_order` decide the order. `glob_patterns` filters
which files are picked up.

## Watch out
Every photo is forced to the target resolution with `crop = center`.
Non-square photos lose their edges. Crop deliberately beforehand if that
matters.

Each run overwrites nothing - the `filename_prefix` counter keeps
counting up. But the maps of photo 3 and photo 4 land in the same folder
with sequential numbers, so keep track of which set belongs together.
The `STRING` output carries the source filenames if you want to route
them somewhere.
